title: Should cities charge for parking space?

turns.speaker: Su
turns.text: Residents' permits go from thirty pounds a year to two hundred and forty, and the letters have started already.

turns.speaker: Cole
turns.text: Thirty pounds a year for a piece of city land is the part that should surprise people, honestly.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: It works out at about eight pence a day for roughly twelve square metres of public space.

turns.speaker: Su
turns.text: Put like that it sounds indefensible.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: It is indefensible. The same square metres as a flat's balcony, and nobody gets that for eight pence.

turns.speaker: Cole
turns.text: The objection that matters is that it's flat. Two hundred and forty means nothing to one household and a lot to another.

turns.speaker: Cole
turns.text: So you get a policy that prices out the people least able to move somewhere better connected.

turns.speaker: Su
turns.text: Which is solvable. Several cities scale it by income or by vehicle size.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: By emissions usually, which correlates with size and sometimes with wealth, though not reliably.

turns.speaker: Cole
turns.text: The cruising evidence is the strongest argument for pricing at all. A large share of central traffic is people looking for a space.

turns.speaker: Su
turns.text: Around a third in some studies, which is an enormous amount of pollution generated by underpricing.

turns.speaker: Marta
turns.text: And the money is supposed to go back into the neighbourhood, which is the part that decides whether anyone accepts it.

turns.speaker: Cole
turns.text: In practice it goes to the general fund and the trust never recovers.

points: Residents' parking permits rise from thirty to two hundred and forty pounds a year.
Marta notes the old price amounted to about eight pence a day for twelve square metres of public land.
Cole's objection is that a flat charge burdens poorer households disproportionately and prices out those least able to move.
Several cities scale charges by income, vehicle size or emissions, though the correlation with wealth is unreliable.
Studies suggest around a third of central traffic is drivers searching for spaces, making underpricing a significant source of pollution.
Acceptance depends on revenue returning to the neighbourhood, which often does not happen.
